title: DAVID HAD WIVES AND CONCUBINES—YET GOD HAD ALREADY WARNED ISRAEL’S KING NOT TO MULTIPLY WIVES
paragraphs: DAVID HAD WIVES AND CONCUBINES—YET GOD HAD ALREADY WARNED ISRAEL’S KING NOT TO MULTIPLY WIVES

David was a man after God’s heart. David also multiplied wives. Both statements are in the Bible. And what happened next should terrify anyone who has ever mistaken God’s patience for God’s permission.
There is a sentence in the Law of Moses that David could not honestly claim he had never needed to hear.
It was written specifically for Israel’s future kings.
Long before David sat on a throne...
Long before Jerusalem became his capital...
Long before Nathan walked into the palace and said, “Thou art the man”...
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself.”
“So that his heart does not turn aside.”
God was not merely regulating the size of a royal household.
God was talking about the king’s heart.
And suddenly this becomes much bigger than an ancient argument about polygamy.
Because you may have only one spouse.
You may never sit on a throne.
But you still have a heart.
And your heart can still be divided.
That is where this story finds us.
Because one of the most dangerous moments in the Christian life is when God has blessed us enough that we begin believing the blessing means He approves of everything we are doing.
David knew what it was to be hunted.
He knew what it felt like to have a spear thrown at him.
He knew what it meant to wait while another man occupied the throne God had promised him.
And then Scripture quietly records something deeply uncomfortable:
“And David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron...” — 2 Samuel 5:13, KJV.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes.
That is one reason you can trust its honesty.
If human beings were inventing propaganda to glorify their national heroes, they would probably remove the adultery, murder, family catastrophe, rebellion, humiliation, tears, and moral failures.
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive men saving themselves.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with sinful humanity...
and ultimately of a Savior coming to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
David's greatness therefore cannot turn David's choices into God's commandments.
The Bible can describe something without prescribing it.
The fact that Scripture tells us David had multiple wives does not mean Scripture commands believers to imitate him.
In fact, the tension becomes sharper when you return to Deuteronomy.
Israel's future king was not supposed to treat kingship like the pagan rulers surrounding him.
He was warned against multiplying horses.
Warned against multiplying silver and gold.
Because God's king was supposed to live under God's Word rather than above it.
And the next instruction is astonishing.
When the king sat upon his throne, he was to make for himself a copy of the Law and live with it, reading it so that he would learn to fear the LORD.
The throne did not exempt him from Scripture.
The crown did not place him above Scripture.
His victories did not place him above Scripture.
His anointing did not place him above Scripture.
His calling did not place him above Scripture.
That may be the sentence somebody reading this needed.
Because success can create a strange spiritual anesthesia.
When everything is falling apart, we search our hearts.
When everything is succeeding, we sometimes stop.
When the bills are unpaid, we pray.
When the account grows, we can forget.
When the relationship is breaking, we cry before God.
When life becomes comfortable, compromise suddenly becomes easier to rename.
And sometimes the most frightening evidence against us is that nothing terrible happened immediately afterward.
David should destroy that illusion forever.
God's patience is not the same thing as God's permission.
Grace is not divine endorsement of sin.
And delayed consequences do not transform disobedience into obedience.
This is also why 2 Samuel 12 must be handled carefully.

After David took Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's death, Nathan confronted him. God reminded David of everything He had given him, including Saul's household and wives, before condemning David for despising God's word and taking Uriah's wife.
Some readers encounter that passage and conclude, “Then God must have approved of polygamy.”
But that conclusion asks the text to say more than it says.

Ancient royal succession involved the transfer of a predecessor's household into the authority and protection of the succeeding king. The passage emphasizes the abundance God had placed under David's rule and the monstrous ingratitude of taking the one woman who belonged to Uriah.
It certainly does not transform “he shall not multiply wives” into “multiply wives.”
Scripture must be allowed to interpret Scripture.
And what makes the warning even more haunting is what happened in the next generation.
Solomon did what David had done...
Scripture records seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines.
Then comes the sentence Deuteronomy had warned about centuries earlier:
His wives turned away his heart.
And now the question becomes uncomfortable.
Maybe your problem is not David's problem.
Maybe there are no concubines hidden in your life.
But maybe there is something you keep adding...
even though somewhere deep inside, you already know God has been telling you:
Another resentment rehearsed in your head.
Another promise that tomorrow you will finally stop.
Another Sunday raising your hands while Monday keeps exposing what you refuse to surrender.
Usually not with someone waking up one morning and declaring, “Today I will destroy my spiritual life.”
It happens one tolerated compromise at a time.
One conviction ignored until the voice that once shook you becomes background noise.
And perhaps the most dangerous words a believer can whisper are:
The prophet tells the king a story.
A rich man has many flocks.
A poor man has one little lamb he loves.
Instead of taking from his abundance, the rich man takes the poor man's lamb.
He can see another man's sin perfectly.
And suddenly David discovers something we all eventually discover:
You can become furious about a sin in someone else while protecting another version of it in yourself.
You can know Scripture and still need Scripture to expose you.
You can worship sincerely and still have something hidden.
You can love God and still disobey God.
You can be genuinely called and genuinely wrong.
You can have a testimony and still need repentance.
But here is where the Gospel enters this story with breathtaking force.
Yet David was not beyond repentance.
When Nathan exposed him, David did not manufacture a public-relations campaign.
He did not say everyone was doing it.
And Psalm 51 lets us hear something even more intimate.
We hear a shattered man asking God for mercy.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV.
That prayer matters because biblical repentance is not merely:
Create in me a clean heart.
David needed something deeper than damage control.
Forgiveness did not make Uriah's blood imaginary.
Grace did not make David's choices harmless.
Repentance did not travel backward through history and make the sin righteous.
This is where many people misunderstand grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace does not rewrite God's commandments to protect our feelings.
Grace rewrites the future of repentant sinners through God's mercy.
And David's story points beyond David.
Because David cannot be the ultimate hero.
A King who would not merely write God's law...
A King whose heart would never turn away.
A King who would face temptation without surrendering to it.
A King who would possess all authority without exploiting the vulnerable.
A King who would not steal another man's bride...
but would give Himself for His bride.
David used royal power and Uriah died.
Jesus possessed ultimate authority and willingly died for sinners.
David cried for a clean heart.
Through Christ, sinners are washed, forgiven, reconciled, and made new.
That is why Christianity cannot finally be about becoming a better David.
You need Someone greater than David.
And maybe you have been reading this thinking about David's wives...
when God has been putting His finger on your secret.
That addiction hidden behind a password.
That relationship you already know is pulling you away from Christ.
That private habit you keep promising God you will quit.
That compromise you defended for so long that you almost stopped feeling conviction.
And maybe that ache in your chest is mercy.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully concealed their scandals.
The cross means your sin is more serious than your excuses have allowed you to believe...
and God's grace is greater than your shame has allowed you to imagine.
Because Christ purchased redemption with His blood.
There is forgiveness for the adulterer who repents.
Forgiveness for the liar who repents.
Forgiveness for the addict who repents.
The hypocrite who finally becomes honest.
The believer who wandered farther than anyone knows.
Because Jesus is mighty to save.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private life.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs tonight.
Send this article to someone who has confused God's patience with God's permission.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from a willing heart and is used faithfully for Gospel ministry.
The person contemplating giving up matters.
So if God has given you the desire and ability to help this ministry continue and expand, prayerfully consider becoming a monthly supporter.
And if financially supporting is not possible, do not carry shame.
There are many ways to participate in spreading biblical truth, and generosity offered to God should come willingly—not through spiritual coercion.
Because the deepest point of David's story was never:
Look how desperately even David needed grace.
The man after God's own heart needed grace.
Maybe that is why Scripture refuses to sanitize him.
Because if David's failures had been erased, you might think your failures disqualified you from ever coming home.
But if David's sins had been celebrated, you might think grace meant holiness did not matter.
And the Savior to whom David's story ultimately points is real.
Jesus does not need you to pretend there was never a scandal.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot control.
Bring Him the memory you cannot erase.
Bring Him the tears you never let anyone see.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified other people would reject.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is the announcement that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross...
and His grace is so astonishing that the cross does not have to be the end of your story.
The warning given to Israel's king still whispers across the centuries:
Do not multiply what will eventually master you.
Do not mistake blessing for permission.
Do not wait for your own Nathan moment before taking God's Word seriously.
And when you discover that you have already wandered...
remember the greater Son of David.
There is still a road home.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but once surrendered to Jesus, it does not get to write the final sentence.
